promptText: What is the key difference between monitoring a typical REST service and monitoring an LLM-backed feature?
options: REST services never need monitoring, only LLM features do

A REST service's health is largely captured by uptime, latency, and error rate because success implies a correct result; an LLM feature can return a fast, well-formed 200 OK response that is nonetheless low-quality, hallucinated, or unsafe, requiring additional layers
LLM features cannot be monitored using Prometheus or Grafana at all
REST services require token-based cost tracking, while LLM features do not
explanation: A traditional service's assumption that 'succeeded correctly or threw an error trying' breaks for generative systems, which is why AI monitoring needs quality and safety layers beyond the operational layer every engineer already knows.

promptText: Why should LLM latency be measured as both time-to-first-token (TTFT) and total generation duration, rather than a single number?
options: TTFT and total duration are always numerically identical, so tracking both is redundant but harmless

TTFT drives perceived responsiveness, especially with streaming, while total duration scales with completion length; a regression in one without the other points to a different root cause, so collapsing both into one number hides which problem you actually have
Only total duration matters for LLM systems; TTFT is a legacy metric from non-streaming APIs
Providers do not expose TTFT, so it can never actually be measured
explanation: A slow model queue versus a naturally longer completion look identical in a single latency number but require different fixes, so splitting the signal is necessary for accurate diagnosis.

promptText: Why is average latency or average cost a misleading metric for LLM systems, and what should be tracked instead?
options: Averages are misleading only for cost, never for latency, so latency averages are fine to use alone

LLM latency and cost distributions are typically heavily right-skewed; an average is dominated by the bulk of cheap, fast requests and can look healthy while a meaningful fraction of users experience much worse behavior, so percentiles (p50/p95/p99) should be tracked instead
Averages should be replaced with a single minimum value, since the best case is what users remember
Averages are accurate but percentiles require a paid Prometheus license to compute
explanation: Percentiles expose the long tail that averages hide, which is exactly the population most likely to have a degraded experience worth protecting.

promptText: Which four layers make up a mature AI monitoring program?
options: Frontend, backend, database, and network
Infrastructure/operational, usage/cost, quality/behavior, and safety/abuse
Development, staging, canary, and production
Unit tests, integration tests, load tests, and chaos tests
explanation: Each layer answers a different question: is the service up and fast; how much are we using and spending; is the model still answering well; and is anything malicious or policy-violating happening — a system can be green on the first two while silently failing the last two.

promptText: What is a 'soft error' in LLM monitoring, as distinct from a hard error?
options: A hard error that has been downgraded in severity by an on-call engineer

A response that completes successfully at the transport level (no HTTP failure, no exception) but is functionally broken, such as an empty completion, a malformed structured output, or an unwarranted refusal
Any error that occurs only during off-peak hours
An error that only affects the frontend UI, never the backend
explanation: Soft errors need their own dedicated counters because no infrastructure layer will ever flag them — they are the LLM-specific reinterpretation of the classic 'errors' golden signal.

promptText: Why is tracking 'finish reason' (stop, length, content-filter, tool-call) worth treating as seriously as tracking HTTP status codes?
options: Finish reason is only useful for billing reconciliation, not for detecting problems
Several finish-reason values indicate a silent failure a status code will never surface — for example, 'length' means the completion was truncated mid-thought with a perfectly healthy 200 response
Finish reason and HTTP status code always carry identical information, so tracking both is redundant
Finish reason is deprecated in modern model provider APIs and should not be relied upon
explanation: A completion cut off by hitting the max-token limit, or interrupted by a content filter, materially harms the user experience while looking completely healthy from an HTTP-status perspective.

promptText: How would you detect that an upstream model provider silently swapped the model behind a stable API alias?
options: This is undetectable in principle, since providers never expose model version information

Tag every metric with the model version/identifier string returned in the provider's response metadata, and watch for that tag's value changing in correlation with shifts in latency, token usage, or quality scores, with no corresponding deploy on your side
Check only your own deployment logs, since provider changes always appear there first
Restart the application server, which forces the provider to reveal its current model version
explanation: Cross-referencing shifts in output-length distribution, cost, or quality scores against the reported model-version tag is the classic way to confirm a provider-side change as the root cause of an otherwise unexplained regression.

promptText: Why must Layer 3 (quality) alerts typically use multi-hour or daily rolling windows, while Layer 1 (latency/error rate) alerts can react within minutes?
options: Quality metrics are computed on a statistical sample, so a low-traffic window can produce very few scored responses; the resulting sampling error means a single hour's dip is often within expected noise, unlike high-volume latency and error-rate signals
Quality alerts are less important than latency alerts, so they are checked less frequently by policy
Daily windows are required because LLM-as-judge calls can only run once per day due to rate limits
There is no technical reason; both should always use the same window length
explanation: Because sampled quality scores have their own margin of error proportional to 1/sqrt(n), a small sample per hour makes short-window quality alerts unreliable, so they need longer, statistically baselined windows to distinguish signal from noise.

promptText: Why can 'tokens per request' alone be a misleading cost metric, even if it stays flat?
options: Token counts are always inaccurate, so any metric derived from them is unreliable

Prompt and completion tokens are frequently priced differently, and different models can differ by an order of magnitude in per-token price, so a routing change to a pricier model can cause a large cost swing that a flat 'tokens per request' chart never reveals
Tokens per request is only relevant to latency, never to cost, so tracking it for cost purposes is a category error
Cost is always directly proportional to request count regardless of token usage
explanation: A cost dashboard needs to track dollar-denominated spend and model mix directly, since token count alone hides differential per-token pricing across models and prompt-vs-completion pricing tiers.

promptText: What is the difference between a leading indicator and a lagging indicator in AI monitoring, with an example of each?
options: A lagging indicator tells you damage has already happened, like a spike in user complaints; a leading indicator gives warning before damage accumulates, like a rising refusal rate suggesting an upstream safety filter got stricter
Leading indicators are always more accurate than lagging indicators
A leading indicator is any metric computed before the request completes, and a lagging indicator is any metric computed afterward
Lagging indicators only apply to cost, and leading indicators only apply to latency
explanation: The entire discipline of good monitoring design is finding leading indicators that correlate tightly enough with lagging outcomes you actually care about that you can act before the damage (cost overrun, lost trust) fully accumulates.

promptText: Why should the LLM-specific store (capturing full prompt/completion text for sampled requests) be architecturally separate from the numeric time-series metrics store?
options: Prometheus technically cannot store any string data under any circumstances

Prompts and completions are large, potentially sensitive text blobs with different retention, access-control, and PII-handling requirements than a latency number, so mixing them into the numeric store applies the wrong data-handling discipline to sensitive content
Separating the stores is purely a performance optimization with no security or governance implication
Numeric metrics and text data cannot physically coexist in the same data center
explanation: Treating the LLM-specific store with the same access-control, encryption, and retention discipline as any system holding customer data is a security requirement, not just an infrastructure convenience.

promptText: Why is tagging a Micrometer counter with a raw user ID or full prompt text dangerous, even though it seems like a useful debugging dimension?
options: It has no real downside; more tag dimensions always improve dashboard usefulness

High-cardinality tags turn a handful of time series into millions of near-empty ones, which most metrics backends including Prometheus handle poorly and can degrade or crash under; per-user or per-prompt detail belongs in the trace/log store instead
Micrometer physically rejects any tag longer than 8 characters
User IDs are considered copyrighted data and cannot legally be stored in any monitoring system
explanation: Coarser dimensions (tenant, feature, model, prompt-template-version) keep cardinality bounded on metrics, while unbounded per-request detail belongs in the separate trace/log store built to handle that kind of uniqueness.

promptText: A quality-score dashboard shows a sudden drop at 3 AM that recovers by 6 AM, with no deploy in that window. What is the correct diagnostic sequence before declaring this a real incident?
options: Immediately page the on-call engineer and roll back the most recent deploy, since any drop in quality score is definitionally an incident
Ignore it entirely, since overnight metrics are never meaningful

First check the sample size behind the score during that low-traffic window (a small sample can produce a dip within expected sampling-error noise); then check whether the dip correlates with a specific tagged dimension (model version, tenant, request type); then check whether Layer 1 or Layer 2 signals moved in the same window, since real provider incidents often show up briefly across multiple layers simultaneously
Assume it is always a provider-side outage without checking any internal signals
explanation: Overnight low traffic combined with fixed sampling can produce very few scored responses, well within statistical noise; only escalate as an incident if the drop exceeds the noise band for that sample size and correlates with another independent signal.

promptText: A support assistant shows 100% uptime, fast p99 latency, and zero exceptions on its Grafana dashboard, yet customers are receiving increasingly hallucinated answers. What does this scenario demonstrate about Layer 1 monitoring?
options: It demonstrates that Layer 1 metrics are unnecessary and should be removed entirely

It demonstrates that Layer 1 (operational) health is necessary but nowhere near sufficient for an AI system — a model that hallucinates more or leaks retrieved PII into responses produces a perfectly healthy-looking 200 OK with fast response time, since none of that shows up as an HTTP error or latency spike
It demonstrates that Grafana is fundamentally incompatible with AI systems and must be replaced
It demonstrates that hallucination rate is actually a subcategory of latency, not a separate concern
explanation: This is the single most common design mistake teams make: declaring an AI feature 'monitored' once infrastructure dashboards are green, while quality (Layer 3) or safety (Layer 4) silently degrades underneath with no operational signal at all.

promptText: A VP asks why the team needs a separate LLM observability tool when Datadog/Grafana already monitor every other service. What is the strongest staff-level justification, and what should be built versus bought?
options: Existing APM tools should be discarded entirely and replaced wholesale by an LLM-specific vendor tool, since the two cannot coexist

Existing APM tools cover Layer 1 (and largely Layer 2) well but were not designed to capture full prompt/completion payloads, token-level cost attribution, or quality/faithfulness scoring; the right approach is to keep numeric operational/cost metrics in the existing Micrometer/Prometheus/Grafana pipeline while adding a thin Advisor-level instrumentation layer that also feeds prompt/completion capture and sampled LLM-as-judge scoring into a system built for that data shape, whether bought or built
No justification is needed, since Datadog and Grafana already capture prompt and completion text natively
The team should build every layer from scratch in-house to avoid any vendor dependency whatsoever
explanation: The justification is 'add the missing layers,' not 'replace what works' — text-shaped, sensitive, high-volume prompt/completion data has different query patterns and sensitivity than a numeric metrics database is optimized for, so building only the thin instrumentation layer avoids vendor lock-in on the underlying metrics pipeline while still closing the AI-specific gap.
